unitDescription.value: In this unit, students investigate how artificial intelligence systems learn from data and how machine learning can be used to classify images and gestures. Using resources from MyComputerBrain and Google Teachable Machine, students explore key AI concepts including training data, classes, confidence, accuracy, testing and bias. Students then design and develop their own sign-language recognition model, collecting and labelling data, training a model, testing its performance and improving it through iteration. Through this project, students learn that AI systems are not simply “smart”, but are shaped by the quality and fairness of the data used to train them. The unit concludes with students presenting a working prototype and evaluating its usefulness, limitations and ethical impact.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: The Years 9–10 cohort consists of a diverse group of boys with a wide range of digital competencies, from students with strong technical skills and personal interest in IT, to those who require further support to confidently engage with digital systems. Many students come from regional or rural backgrounds, where access to structured digital learning opportunities may have been limited. The program is designed to build on prior knowledge while introducing more advanced and applied skills relevant to future study and employment. The curriculum supports the school’s priority to equip students with transferable digital skills, critical thinking abilities, and an understanding of ethical technology use in a rapidly changing world.

description.value: Students design and develop an original sign-language recognition model using machine learning principles. They act as developers to collect and label representative training data, configure and train their model within a development environment, and iteratively test and refine its performance to improve accuracy. Students document their technical process in a logbook, including data cleaning strategies and model optimization. The project concludes with a working prototype demonstration, accompanied by an evaluation of the system’s effectiveness, limitations, and ethical implications, specifically addressing data bias and the Australian Privacy Principles.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students develop and modify innovative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and critically evaluate alternative solutions against stakeholder elicited user stories. Students acquire, interpret and model complex data with databases and represent documents as content, structure and presentation. They design and validate algorithms and implement them, including in an object-oriented programming language. Students explain how digital systems manage, control and secure access to data; and model cyber security threats and explore a vulnerability. They use advanced features of digital tools to create interactive content, and to plan, collaborate on, and manage agile projects. Students apply privacy principles to manage digital footprints.

activities.title: Key Vocabulary of AI Fairness
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define core concepts: Algorithmic bias (systematic errors in computer systems that create unfair outcomes), Representative data (a sample that accurately reflects the diversity of the target population), and Overfitting (model memorising training data rather than generalising). Expected: The training data was non-representative, meaning the model never learned the distinct facial feature weights for diverse users. What if an AI model is trained using photos taken only in bright daylight? Expected: It will fail to classify images correctly under indoor or low-light conditions.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions provided: 1. Algorithmic bias = systematic and repeatable errors in a computer system that create unfair outcomes. 2. Representative data = a dataset that accurately reflects all potential users and environmental conditions.
activities.eLearning: Laptops down. Direct student focus to the whiteboard definitions before independent workbook completion.
activities.transition: Direct students to transition from the vocabulary table to the structured case study analysis.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Algorithmic bias: Systematic errors creating unfair outcomes. 2. Representative data: Dataset reflecting full population diversity. 3. Overfitting: Model memorising training examples rather than generalising. 4. Data diversity: Inclusion of varied lighting, angles, and users.
